_comment: Fault families for the maximal instep (laces) drive, with machine-evaluable signatures over kick_metrics metric ids and derived sequencing events. Evaluated by gateway/kick_faults.py BEFORE any model call; the observe stage confirms or rejects candidates. Thresholds are deliberately conservative (they fire on clear deviations, not marginal ones) because a false candidate costs model attention while a missed one is still findable from the raw table. Normalized units are a fraction of athlete pixel height, so 0.06 is about 10 cm for a 1.7 m athlete. Angles: knee/hip are INTERIOR angles where 180 = fully straight; trunk_lean is positive toward the target, so skilled backward lean is NEGATIVE. Cues are a menu to adapt, never to copy verbatim: cue-style evidence is genuinely mixed in youth (see kick_biomechanics.md), so each family mixes external-focus, analogy, and direct phrasings.

faults.name: Plant foot lands behind the ball
faults.why: Skilled kickers plant level with or slightly ahead of ball centre (about 0.10 m ahead). Fore-aft plant position governs ball TRAJECTORY far more than ball speed: planting behind the ball tilts the instep upward and lofts the strike. Do not sell this as a power fix — a plus-or-minus 15 cm fore-aft shift showed no significant effect on ball velocity.
cues: Step past the ball as you plant, not short of it.
Land your plant foot level with the ball, not behind it.
Drive your body over the ball before you swing through.
Feel your chest arrive above the ball at the strike.
Take a longer last stride so you arrive beside the ball.

faults.name: Plant foot lands well past the ball
faults.why: Overrunning the ball forces the kicking leg to reach backward for contact, cutting the swing short and pulling the strike off the intended line. Measured elite fore-aft offset is about 0.10 m ahead, not a stride ahead. Like its mirror fault, this mainly changes trajectory and strike quality rather than raw ball speed.
cues: Plant beside the ball, not past it, to keep your balance.
Shorten your last step so the plant foot lands level.
Stop your run beside the ball rather than striding through it.
Keep the ball beside your plant foot, not behind your hips.

faults.name: Kicking knee never folds deeply enough
faults.why: Skilled kickers fold the kicking knee to roughly 90-120 degrees of flexion (about 60-90 degrees interior) during leg cocking. A shallow fold shortens the runway over which the shank can be accelerated, so the foot never reaches striking speed.
cues: Snap your heel up toward your backside before swinging through.
Fold the kicking leg tight like a coiled spring.
Let your heel travel higher behind you before the strike.
Load a deeper bend in the kicking knee first.

faults.name: Segments fire out of order (no whip)
faults.why: The instep kick is organised proximal-to-distal: the thigh peaks first and decelerates toward zero at impact while the shank peaks last and fastest. When that order breaks the leg swings as one rigid lever, and the velocity amplification that makes the foot travel two to three times faster than the thigh never happens. Coach the ORDER, not thigh braking: whether thigh deceleration causes shank acceleration is disputed, and the deceleration may itself be an effect of the shank swinging forward.
cues: Lead with the thigh, then whip the lower leg through.
Think crack a whip: hip first, foot arrives last.
Start the swing from your hip, not your knee.
Drive the knee forward first and let the foot follow.

faults.name: Kicking foot is slow into the ball
faults.why: Foot speed at contact is the single strongest determinant of ball speed (r above 0.74). Low foot speed is a SYMPTOM, so read it alongside the sequencing events and backswing depth rather than coaching it in isolation. The signature is deliberately keyed to stature-normalized speed, not m/s: an absolute adult-elite threshold flags every smaller athlete as deficient purely for being small.
cues: Swing faster through the ball, finishing high and long.
Accelerate the foot into the ball and finish high.
Build speed through the whole run, not just the kick.
Kick through the ball toward a point beyond it.

faults.name: Leg is nearly straight at ball contact
faults.why: The knee is NOT extended at contact in skilled kickers: it stays roughly 40-60 degrees flexed (about 120-140 degrees interior), reaching full extension only during follow-through. A straight leg at contact means the athlete reached for the ball and the knee extensors have already finished their work.
cues: Strike with the knee still bent, not a straight leg.
Stop reaching for the ball; let it come to you.
Keep a bend in the kicking knee through contact.
Meet the ball slightly closer so the leg stays loaded.

faults.name: Chest falls forward over the ball at contact
faults.why: Skilled kickers are inclined BACKWARD roughly 12-18 degrees at ball contact; the trunk is an active energy-transfer link, not a passive strut. Falling forward closes the space the kicking leg needs and drives the strike down into the ground.
cues: Lean your chest back slightly as you strike the ball.
Let your shoulders sit behind the ball at contact.
Stay tall and lean away as the foot arrives.
Feel your chest open to the sky through the strike.

faults.name: Plant leg collapses under the strike
faults.why: The support knee sits around 42 degrees of flexion at ball contact (about 138 degrees interior) and begins extending just before it. A more extended, stiffer support leg is associated with faster foot speed and better accuracy; a collapsing one absorbs the energy the run-up generated.
cues: Plant a firm leg and push the ground away.
Keep the plant leg strong and tall through the strike.
Push the ground away with the plant foot as you kick.
Stay tall on the plant leg instead of sinking down.

faults.name: Opposite arm stays pinned to the body
faults.why: The non-kicking-side arm abducts to roughly 48 degrees at impact and travels through far more range than in an ordinary running stride. It carries angular momentum opposing the kicking leg's, and greater non-kicking-arm momentum is a feature of more forceful kicks.
cues: Spread the opposite arm wide to balance the swinging leg.
Let your arms fly out like wings as you strike.
Open the arm across your body for balance.
Reach the opposite arm out wide through contact.

faults.name: Swing stops at the ball
faults.why: Follow-through is about a quarter of the whole kick, ending with the kicking hip flexed to roughly 85-97 degrees. A truncated finish most often means an accuracy-constrained or submaximal effort rather than a discrete defect, so check the athlete's intent before coaching it.
cues: Finish with the kicking leg high toward the target.
Follow through until your body carries past the ball.
Keep swinging after contact instead of stopping at the ball.
Land forward on the kicking foot after the strike.

faults.name: Body weight never gets over the ball
faults.why: Energy is transferred from the support leg and torso into the pelvis and then to the kicking leg; the whole-body centre of mass has to travel through the strike for that chain to load. A trunk centre of mass parked well behind the ball means the athlete is kicking with the leg alone.
cues: Carry your body over the ball as you strike it.
Move your weight forward through the strike, not backward.
Arrive with your chest above the ball at contact.
Push your hips toward the target through the kick.
